title: Henry Ford's First Car Company Folds, and He Builds a Racer
dek: The Detroit Automobile Company built no more than twenty vehicles before dissolving in January 1901; Ford set out to win back his backers with a race car.

story.company: Detroit Automobile Company (later Henry Ford Company, then Cadillac)
story.event: The dissolution of his first car company and his turn to a racing car to restore his standing
story.summary: Henry Ford left the Edison Illuminating Company in August 1899 to be superintendent of the Detroit Automobile Company, backed by William H. Murphy and other investors; it built no more than twenty vehicles and was dissolved in January 1901. With Murphy paying much of the cost, Ford built the racer Sweepstakes and beat Alexander Winton at Grosse Pointe on 10 October 1901, which brought backing for the Henry Ford Company; he left it in March 1902 and founded Ford Motor Company in 1903.
paragraphs: On 29 October 1900, Henry Ford received what appears to have been his last salary cheque from the Detroit Automobile Company, for $75. Fourteen months earlier he had resigned as chief engineer of the Edison Illuminating Company, turning down a promised $1,900 a year, to become the new firm's superintendent at $150 a month. Its main financial backer was William H. Murphy. Ford had no personal funds; his wife, he later wrote, agreed "that we had to make or break."

The work did not go as planned. The first product, a delivery wagon finished in January 1900, drew a glowing write-up in the Detroit News-Tribune, but curators at The Henry Ford museum judge it was not a very good vehicle. Ford, the historian Ford R. Bryan noted, had never made more than one car at a time. The company built no more than twenty trucks and cars, not to the quality Ford wanted and too dear to sell, and it was formally dissolved in January 1901.

Ford's own account, written two decades later, was that his backers cared more about building to order at the highest price than about better cars. The company, he wrote, was "merely a money-making concern--that did not make much money." His backers, the museum's curators say, now doubted him as an engineer and as a businessman.

He chose to answer with speed. Through 1901, with friends helping part-time, he built a light two-cylinder racing car; Murphy covered much of its reported cost of about $5,000. On 10 October 1901, on a horse-racing track at Grosse Pointe, Ford raced it against Alexander Winton, the country's best-known driver. He trailed by as much as 300 yards until Winton's car developed mechanical trouble, then swept past. "The people went wild," Clara Ford wrote to her brother.

Murphy and other investors formed the Henry Ford Company that November. Ford soon fell out with them and left in March 1902 with $900, a racer's drawings and the use of his name; reorganised around Henry Leland, the firm became Cadillac. Ford Motor Company followed in June 1903. In his memoir Ford folded his first two companies into one story, ending with a resignation "determined never again to put myself under orders."

quote.text: Although men flatter themselves with their great actions, they are not so often the result of a great design as of chance.
quote.work: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims
quote.source_title: Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims, tr. J. Hain Friswell, Project Gutenberg eBook #9105
quote.connection: Ford's memoir tells these years as a lesson he drew by design: never again to work under other people's orders. La Rochefoucauld would point to the race that rescued him, won after Winton's car broke down. How much of what followed was judgment and how much was luck stays open.

reflection: When something you started ends badly, the account you give yourself afterwards shapes what you try next. Ford's account was tidy: the backers wanted money, he wanted better cars. It left out that he had never built more than one car at a time, and that his second chance came partly from a rival's failing engine.

You do not need a tidy story about your setbacks. A fair one is more use: what was yours to change, what belonged to other people, and what was simply luck. The last part is the one people most often leave out, in failure and in success alike.
invitation: Think of one setback from this year and write a single honest sentence about the part of it that was plain bad luck. Notice whether that sentence was hard to write, and leave it there for today.

cross_checks.claim: Ford left the Edison Illuminating Company in August 1899 to work for the new Detroit Automobile Company.
The Detroit Automobile Company built no more than about twenty vehicles and was dissolved in January 1901.
Its first product was a delivery wagon completed in January 1900.
On 10 October 1901 at Grosse Pointe Ford beat Alexander Winton after Winton's car developed mechanical trouble.
Ford left the Henry Ford Company in March 1902 and it became Cadillac.

research_notes: Founding date: 5 August 1899 (Bryan/HFHA, automotivehistory.org) versus July 1899 (The Henry Ford's collection records); the story gives no founding date. Dissolution: January 1901 (Bryan; The Henry Ford's records); automotivehistory.org says the company dissolved after about 20 vehicles 'by November 1900'; the 2021 Henry Ford curators' article says it had failed 'by summer 1901'; Wikipedia (not cited) gives both January 1901 and a November 1901 reorganisation. The story uses January 1901 and does not date the backers' doubts. Vehicles: 'no more than 20' (The Henry Ford), 'about 20' (automotivehistory.org), 'nineteen or twenty' (Ford's memoir); the story says no more than twenty. Henry Ford Company: formed 30 November 1901 (Bryan) or November 1901 (automotivehistory.org); The Henry Ford's lesson page says 1902; the story says 'that November'. Ford's memoir (1922) merges the two companies: it says he worked three years with the Detroit Automobile Company and resigned in March 1902, but the March 1902 resignation was from the Henry Ford Company (Bryan); the story says so explicitly. The $75 cheque is hedged as in Bryan ('what appears to have been his final check'). Causes: automotivehistory.org attributes the failure to Ford's perfectionism and Bryan mentions stockholders in a hurry for profits; following the rule to attribute blame only as the founder himself put it, the story gives Ford's own account, labelled as his, alongside neutral facts (the vehicles' quality and price, his lack of experience making more than one car at a time). Funding set to 'venture' rather than the slate's 'mixed': the company was financed by outside investors (Murphy and fellow stockholders) and Ford had no personal funds to invest, by his own account. Clara Ford's letter is quoted from The Henry Ford's 2021 article. History Today's 1999 piece blocked WebFetch and is not cited. La Rochefoucauld's Maxim 57 is about great actions in general and is applied here by analogy.
